source_text: Quibus ex rebus cum constet illos homines fuisse, non est obscurum qua ratione dii coeperint nominari. si enim nulli reges ante Saturnum uel Uranum fuerunt propter hominum raritatem, qui agrestem uitam sine ullo rectore uiuebant, non est dubium quin illis temporibus homines regem ipsum totamque gentem mactare summis laudibus ac nonis honoribus coeperint, ut etiam deos appellarent siue ob miraculum uirtutis — hoc uere putabant rudes adhuc et simplices — siue, ut fieri solet, in adulationem praesentis potentiae siue ob beneficia quibus erant ad humanitatem conpositi. deinde ipsi reges cum cari fuissent iis quorum uitam composuerant, magnum sui desiderium mortui reliquerunt. itaque homines eorum simulacra finxerunt, ut haberent aliquod ex imaginum contemplatione solacium, progressique longius per amorem memoriam defunctorum colere coeperunt, ut et gratiam referre bene meritis uiderentur et successores eorum adlicerent ad bene imperandi cupiditatem. quod Cicero de natura deorum docet dicens: suscepit autem uita hominum consuetudoque communis, ut beneficiis excellentis uiros in caelum fama ac uoluntate tollerent. hinc Hercules, hinc Castor, hinc Pollux, hinc Aesculapius, hinc Liber. et alio loco: atque in plerisque ciuitatibus intellegi potest acuendae uirtutis gratia aut quo libentius rei publicae causa periculum adiret optimus quisque, uirorum fortium memoriam honore deorum inmortalium consecratam. hac scilicet ratione Romani Caesares suos consecrauerunt et Mauri suos reges. sic paulatim religiones esse coeperunt, dum illi primi qui eos nouerant eo ritu suos liberos ac nepotes, deinde omnes posteros imbuerunt, et hi tandem summi reges ob celebritatem nominis in prouinciis omnibus colebantur. priuatim uero singuli populi gentis aut urbis suae conditores, seu uiri fortitudine insignes erant seu feminae castitate mirabiles, summa ueneratione coluerunt, ut Aegyptus Isidem, Mauri Iubam, Macedones Cabirum, Poeni Uraniam, Latini Faunum, Sabini Sancum, Romani Quirinum, eodem utique modo Athenae Mineruam, Samos Iunonem, Paphos Venerem, Vulcanum Lemnos, Liberum Naxos, Apollinem Delos. sic per populos atque regiones uaria sacra suscepta sunt, dum homines grati esse in suos principes cupiunt et quos alios honores uita carentibus deferant, inuenire non possunt. praeterea pietas eorum qui successerant plurimum contulit ad errorem: qui ut • diuina stirpe nati uiderentur, diuinos honores parentibus detulerunt deferrique iusserunt. an potest aliquis dubitare, quomodo religiones deorum sint institutae, cum apud Maronem legat Aeneae uerba sociis imperantis: nunc pateras libate Ioui precibusque uocate Anchisen genitorem —? cui non tantum immortalitatem, uerum etiam uentorum tribuit potestatem: poscamus uentos, atque haec me sacra quotannis urbe uelit posita templis sibi ferre dicatis. idem scilicet de Ioue Liber et Pan et Mercurius et Apollo fecerunt ac postea de his ipsis successores eorum. accesserunt etiam poetae et compositis ad uoluptatem carminibus in caelum eos sustulerunt, sicut faciunt qui apud reges etiam malos panegyricis mendacibus adulantur. quod malum a Graecis ortum est, quorum leuitas instructa dicendi facultate et copia incredibile est quantas mendaciorum nebulas excitauerit. itaque admirati eos et susceperunt primi sacra illorum et uniuersis gentibus tradiderunt. ob hanc uanitatem Sibylla sic eos increpat: Ἑλλὰς δὴ, τί πέποιθας ἐπ᾽ ἀνδράσιν ἡγεμόνεσσι; πρὸς τί δὲ δῶρα μάταια καταφθιμένοις πορίζεις; θύεις εἰδώλοις; τίς σοι πλάνον ἐν φρεσὶ θῆκεν ταῦτα τελεῖν προλιπόντα θεοῦ μεγάλοιο πρόσωπον. M. Tullius, qui non tantum perfectus orator, sed etiam philosophus fuit, siquidem solus extitit Platonis imitator, in eo libro quo se ipse de morte filiae consolatus est, non dubitauit dicere deos qui publice colerentur homines fuisse. quod ipsius testimonium eo debet grauissimum iudicari, quod et augurale habuit sacerdotium et eosdem se colere uenerarique testatur. itaque intra paucos uersiculos duas res nobis dedit. nam dum imaginem filiae eodem se modo consecraturum esse profitetur quo illi a ueteribus sint consecrati, et illos mortuos esse docuit et originem uanae superstitionis ostendit. cum uero inquit et mares et feminas complures ex hominibus in deorum numero esse uideamus et eorum in urbibus atque agris augustissima delubra ueneremur, adsentiamur eorum sapientiae quorum ingeniis et inuentis omnem uitam legibus et institutis excultam constitutamque habemus. quod si ullum umquam animal consecrandum fuit, illud profecto fuit. si Cadmi progenies aut Amphitryonis aut Tyndari in caelum tollenda fama fuit, huic idem honos certe dicandus est. quod quidem faciam teque omnium optimam doctissimam adprobantibus diis inmortalibus ipsis in eorum coetu locatam ad opinionem omnium mortalium consecrabo. fortasse dicat aliquis prae nimio luctu delirasse Ciceronem. atquin illa omnis oratio et doctrina et exemplis et ipso loquendi genere perfecta non aegri, sed constantis animi ac iudicii fuit et haec ipsa sententia nullum praefert indicium doloris. neque enim puto illum tali uarie, tam copiose, tam ornate scribere potuisse, nisi luctum eius et ratio ipsa et consolatio amicorum et longitudo temporis mitigasset. quid quod idem dicit in libris de re publica, idem de gloria? nam de legibus, quo in opere Platonem secutus leges uoluit ponere, quibus putaret usuram esse iustam et sapientem ciuitatem, de religione ita sanxit: diuos et eos qui caelestes semper habiti sunt colunto et ollos quos endo caelo merita locauerunt, Herculem Liberum Aesculapium Castorem Pollucem Quirinum. item in Tusculanis, cum diceret totum paene caelum humano genere conpletum, si uero inquit scrutari uetera et ex illis ea quae scriptores Graeciae prodiderunt eruere coner, ipsi illi maiorum gentium di qui habentur hinc a nobis profecti in caelum reperientur. quare quoniam demonstrantur sepulchra in Graecia, reminiscere, quoniam es initiatus, quae tradantur mysteriis: tum denique quam hoc late pateat intelleges. testatus est uidelicet Attici conscientiam, ex ipsis mysteriis intellegi posse quod omnes illi homines fuerint qui coluntur, et cum de Hercule Libero Aesculapio Castore Polluce incunctanter fateretur, de Apolline ac Ioue patribus eorum, item de Neptuno Uulcano Marte Mercurio, quos maiorum gentium deos appellauit, timuit aperte coner. et idcirco ait late hocpatere, ut idem de Ioue ceterisque antiquioribus diis intellegamus, quorum memoriam si eadem ratione ueteres consecrauerunt, qua se imaginem nomenque filiae consecraturum esse dicit, ignosci maerentibus potest, credentibus non potest. quis enim tam demens, qui consensu et plaCitO innumerabilium stultorum aperiri caelum mortuis arbitretur aut aliquem quod ipse non habeat dare alteri posse? apud Romanos deus Iulius, quia hoc scele- rato homini placuit Antonio, deus Quirinus, quia hoc pastoribus uisum est, cum alter gemini fratris extiterit, alter patriae parricida. quodsi non consul fuisset Antonius, Gaius Caesar pro suis in rem publicam meritis etiam defuncti hominis honore caruisset, et quidem consilio Pisonis soceri et Lucii Caesaris propinqui, qui uetabant funus ei fieri, et Dolabellae consulis, qui columnam in foro id est tumulum eius euertit ac forum expiauit. nam Romulum desiderio suis fuisse declarat Ennius, apud quem populus amissum regem dolens haec loquitur: o Romule, Romule die, qualem te patriae custodem di genuerunt! tu produxisti nos intra luminis oras, o pater, o genitor, o sanguen dis oriundum. ob hoc desiderium facilius creditum est Iulio Proculo mentienti, qui subornatus a patribus est, ut nuntiaret plebi uidisse se regem humano habitu augustiorem eumque mandasse ad populum, ut sibi delubrum fieret, se deum esse et Quirinum uocari. quo facto et ipsi populo persuasit Romulum ad deos abisse et senatum suspicione caedis regiae liberauit.
pass_a_gloss: From which things, since it is established that those men were, it is not obscure by what reason they began to be named gods. For if there were no kings before Saturn or Uranus because of the rarity of men, who lived a rustic life without any ruler, there is no doubt that in those times men began to sacrifice the king himself and the whole nation with the greatest praises and honors, so that they even called them gods, either because of the miracle of virtue — this they truly believed, being still rude and simple — or, as it usually happens, in flattery of present power or because of the benefits by which they were composed to humanity. Then, when the kings themselves had been dear to those whose life they had composed, they left a great longing for themselves when they died. And so, men made images of them, so that they might have some solace from the contemplation of the images, and, progressing further through love, they began to honor the memory of the dead, so that they might seem to repay gratitude to the well-deserving and entice their successors to the desire of ruling well. Which Cicero teaches, saying: The life of men and common custom, however, took up the practice of elevating excellent men to heaven by fame and will because of their benefits. From this, Hercules, Castor, Pollux, Aesculapius, Liber. And in another place: And in most cities, it can be understood that for the sake of sharpening virtue or so that the best men might more readily undertake danger for the sake of the republic, the memory of strong men has been consecrated with the honor of immortal gods. By this reason, the Roman Caesars consecrated their own, and the Moors their kings. Thus, little by little, religions began to exist, while those first ones who knew them imbued their own children and grandchildren, and then all their posterity, with this rite, and these, finally, the highest kings were worshipped in all provinces because of the fame of their name. But privately, individual peoples worshipped the founders of their nation or city, or men notable for strength or women remarkable for chastity, with the greatest veneration, as the Egyptians Isis, the Moors Iuba, the Macedonians Cabirus, the Carthaginians Urania, the Latins Faunus, the Sabines Sancus, the Romans Quirinus, in the same way the Athenians Minerva, the Samians Juno, the Paphians Venus, the Lemnians Vulcan, the Naxians Liber, the Delians Apollo. Thus, various sacred rites were taken up through peoples and regions, while men desired to be grateful to their princes and could not find other honors to confer on those who lacked life. Moreover, the piety of those who succeeded contributed much to the error: who, so that they might seem to have been born of divine stock, gave divine honors to their parents and ordered them to be worshipped. Can anyone doubt how the religions of the gods were instituted, when we read among the words of Maro, Aeneas commanding his companions: Now, let us libate to Jupiter with prayers and invoke Anchises as our father —? To whom not only immortality but also the power of the winds is attributed: Let us ask for winds, and let us declare that these sacred rites, which I have established in the city, in the temples, be brought to him every year. The same was done by Liber, Pan, Mercury, and Apollo, and afterwards by their successors. Poets also added to this, and with composed songs for pleasure, they elevated them to heaven, just as those who flatter even bad kings with mendacious panegyrics. This evil originated among the Greeks, whose frivolity, instructed in the faculty of speaking and abundance, is incredible how many clouds of falsehoods it stirred up. And so, admiring them, they took up their sacred rites and handed them down to all nations. Because of this vanity, the Sibyl thus rebukes them: O Greece, what have you trusted in, relying on leaders of men? Why do you offer vain gifts to the dead? Do you sacrifice to idols? What plan has been placed in your minds to perform these things, having abandoned the face of the great God? M. Tullius, who was not only a perfect orator but also a philosopher, since he alone was an imitator of Plato, in that book in which he consoled himself about the death of his daughter, did not hesitate to say that the gods who are publicly worshipped were men. Which testimony of his ought to be judged most serious, because he also held the augural priesthood and testifies that he worshipped and venerated them. And so, within a few verses, he gave us two things. For while he professes that he will consecrate the image of his daughter in the same way as those who were consecrated by the ancients, he teaches that they were dead and shows the origin of vain superstition. When, indeed, he says that we see many men and women from among men in the number of the gods and that we venerate their most august temples in cities and fields, let us agree with the wisdom of those whose genius and inventions we have, with all life cultivated and established by laws and institutions. Which, if any animal was to be consecrated, this one, surely, was. If the offspring of Cadmus or Amphitryon or Tyndareus was to be elevated to heaven by fame, then this same honor ought to be given to her. Which I will do, and, with the approval of the immortal gods themselves, I will place you, most excellent and learned, in their assembly, in the opinion of all mortals, I will consecrate. Perhaps someone will say that Cicero delirated because of excessive grief. But that whole speech and doctrine, perfect in examples and in the very genre of speaking, was of a constant mind and judgment, and this very sentence shows no sign of grief. For I do not think that he could have written such things so variedly, so copiously, so ornately, unless his grief had been mitigated by reason itself and the consolation of friends and the length of time. What about the fact that he says the same thing in his books On the Republic, the same thing On Glory? For in his book On the Laws, in which he followed Plato, wanting to establish laws by which he thought a city would be just and wise, he sanctioned religion thus: Let them worship the gods and those who have always been considered heavenly, and let them worship those whom merit has placed in heaven, Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, Pollux, Quirinus. Similarly, in his Tusculan Disputations, when he was saying that almost the whole heaven is filled with the human race, if, indeed, we try to investigate ancient things and to draw out from them those things which the writers of Greece have produced, we will find that those very gods of the nations, who are considered to have come from here, have gone to heaven. Wherefore, since their tombs are shown in Greece, remember, since you have been initiated, what is handed down in the mysteries: then, finally, you will understand how far this extends. He testified, namely, to the conscience of Atticus, that it can be understood from the very mysteries that all those who are worshipped were men, and when he was confessing without hesitation about Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, and Pollux, about Apollo and Jupiter, the fathers of these, and also about Neptune, Vulcan, Mars, and Mercury, whom he called the gods of the nations, he was afraid to try openly. And therefore, he says that this extends far, so that we may understand the same thing about Jupiter and the other, more ancient gods, whose memory, if the ancients consecrated in the same way as he says he will consecrate the image and name of his daughter, can be forgiven to the grieving but not to the believing. For who is so foolish as to think that the consensus and pleasure of innumerable fools can open heaven to the dead or that anyone can give what he himself does not have to another? Among the Romans, Julius was made a god because it pleased that wicked man Antony, Quirinus was made a god because it seemed so to the shepherds, when one was the twin brother, the other the parricide of his fatherland. But if Antony had not been consul, Gaius Caesar would have lacked the honor of a dead man for his merits to the republic, and indeed by the counsel of his father-in-law Piso and his relative Lucius Caesar, who forbade his funeral, and of the consul Dolabella, who overthrew the column, that is, the tomb of Caesar, in the forum and expiated the forum. For Ennius declares that Romulus was desired by his people, among whom the people, grieving for their lost king, speak thus: O Romulus, Romulus, say, what kind of guardian of the fatherland the gods generated you to be! You brought us within the boundaries of light, O father, O generator, O blood descended from the gods. Because of this longing, it was more easily believed when Julius Proculus lied, who was suborned by the fathers to announce to the people that he had seen the king in human attire, more majestic, and that he had commanded the people to make a temple for him, saying that he was a god and was to be called Quirinus. By which deed, he also persuaded the people that Romulus had gone to the gods and freed the senate from the suspicion of regicide.

pass_b_english: Since it is established that those men existed, the reason they began to be called gods is clear. No kings ruled before Saturn or Uranus because the human race was sparse and lived a rustic life without any ruler; therefore, it is certain that in those times people began to offer the highest praises and honors to the king himself and the whole nation, so that they even called them gods — whether because of the miracle of their virtue, which those rude and simple people truly believed, or, as often happens, in flattery of present power or because of the benefits by which they had been brought to civilization. Later, because the kings themselves had been dear to those whose lives they had ordered, they left behind a great longing for themselves when they died. Consequently, people fashioned their images so they might find some solace in contemplating them, and, advancing further through love, they began to honor the memory of the dead — both to seem to repay gratitude to the well-deserving and to entice their successors to desire good rule. Cicero teaches this in On the Nature of the Gods, saying: 'The life of men and common custom took up the practice of elevating excellent men to heaven by fame and will because of their benefits.' From this came Hercules, Castor, Pollux, Aesculapius, and Liber. In another place he writes: 'In most cities it can be understood that, for the sake of sharpening virtue or so that the best men might more readily undertake danger for the republic, the memory of strong men has been consecrated with the honor of immortal gods.' By this reasoning the Roman Caesars consecrated their own, and the Moors their kings. Thus religions gradually came into being, while those who first knew them imbued their children and grandchildren, and then all their posterity, with this rite, until finally the highest kings were worshipped in every province because of the fame of their names. Privately, individual peoples worshipped the founders of their nation or city — whether men distinguished by strength or women remarkable for chastity — with the greatest veneration: the Egyptians Isis, the Moors Iuba, the Macedonians Cabirus, the Carthaginians Urania, the Latins Faunus, the Sabines Sancus, the Romans Quirinus; likewise the Athenians Minerva, the Samians Juno, the Paphian Venus, the Lemnians Vulcan, the Naxians Liber, the Delians Apollo. In this way various sacred rites were adopted among peoples and regions, because people desired to be grateful to their princes but could find no other honors to confer on those who lacked life.

Moreover, the piety of those who succeeded contributed greatly to the error: so that they might appear to be born of divine stock, they gave divine honors to their parents and ordered them to be worshipped. Can anyone doubt how the religions of the gods were instituted, when we read in Vergil that Aeneas commanded his companions: 'Now let us libate to Jupiter with prayers and invoke Anchises as our father'? To Anchises was attributed not only immortality but also power over the winds: 'Let us ask for winds, and let us declare that these sacred rites, which I have established in the city and temples, be brought to him every year.' Liber, Pan, Mercury, and Apollo did the same, and afterwards their successors. Poets added to this, lifting them to heaven with songs composed for pleasure, just as those who flatter even bad kings with mendacious panegyrics. This evil originated among the Greeks, whose frivolity, armed with rhetorical skill and abundance of speech, stirred up incredible clouds of falsehoods. And so, admiring them, people adopted their sacred rites and handed them down to all nations. Because of this vanity the Sibyl rebukes them: 'O Greece, what have you trusted, relying on leaders of men? Why do you offer vain gifts to the dead? Do you sacrifice to idols? What delusion has been placed in your minds to perform these things, abandoning the face of the great God?' M. Tullius Cicero — not only a perfect orator but also a philosopher, indeed the sole imitator of Plato — in the book in which he consoled himself for the death of his daughter, did not hesitate to say that the gods publicly worshipped were men. His testimony must be judged most serious, because he also held the augural priesthood and testifies that he himself worshipped and venerated them. In a few verses he gave us two things: while professing that he would consecrate the image of his daughter in the same way as those who were consecrated by the ancients, he taught that they were dead and revealed the origin of vain superstition. When he says that we see many men and women from among humans in the number of the gods, and that we venerate their most august temples in cities and fields, let us agree with the wisdom of those whose genius and inventions have given us a life fully cultivated and established by laws and institutions. If any creature was ever to be consecrated, surely it was she. If the offspring of Cadmus or Amphitryon or Tyndareus was to be elevated to heaven by fame, then this same honor ought to be given to her. I will do so, and with the approval of the immortal gods themselves I will place you, most excellent and learned, in their assembly, consecrating you in the opinion of all mortals.

Perhaps someone will say that Cicero delirated from excessive grief. But that entire speech — perfect in doctrine, examples, and the very manner of speaking — came from a steady mind and judgment, and this very statement shows no sign of grief. I do not think he could have written so variedly, so copiously, so ornately unless his grief had been mitigated by reason itself, the consolation of friends, and the length of time. What about the fact that he says the same thing in On the Republic, the same thing in On Glory? For in On the Laws, where he followed Plato in wanting to establish laws by which a city would be just and wise, he sanctioned religion thus: 'Let them worship the gods and those who have always been considered heavenly, and let them worship those whom merit has placed in heaven — Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, Pollux, Quirinus.' Similarly, in the Tusculan Disputations, when he was saying that almost the whole heaven is filled with the human race, he adds: 'If indeed we try to investigate ancient things and draw out from them what the writers of Greece have produced, those very gods of the nations who are considered to have come from here will be found to have gone to heaven.' Therefore, since their tombs are shown in Greece, remember — since you have been initiated — what is handed down in the mysteries: then you will finally understand how far this extends. He testified to the conscience of Atticus that it can be understood from the very mysteries that all those who are worshipped were men; and when he confessed without hesitation about Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, and Pollux, about Apollo and Jupiter as their fathers, and also about Neptune, Vulcan, Mars, and Mercury, whom he called the gods of the nations, he was afraid to speak openly. That is why he says this extends far, so that we may understand the same thing about Jupiter and the other more ancient gods, whose memory — if the ancients consecrated it in the same way as he says he will consecrate the image and name of his daughter — can be forgiven to the grieving but not to the believing. For who is so foolish as to think that the consensus and applause of innumerable fools can open heaven to the dead, or that anyone can give what he himself does not have to another? Among the Romans, Julius was made a god because it pleased that wicked man Antony; Quirinus was made a god because it seemed so to the shepherds, when one was the twin brother and the other the parricide of his fatherland. Ennius declares that Romulus was desired by his people, among whom the people, grieving for their lost king, speak: 'O Romulus, Romulus, tell us what kind of guardian of the fatherland the gods generated you to be! You brought us within the boundaries of light, O father, O begetter, O blood descended from the gods.' Because of this longing, it was more easily believed when Julius Proculus lied — he had been suborned by the fathers to announce to the people that he had seen the king in human attire, more majestic, and that the king had commanded them to build a temple for him, saying he was a god and was to be called Quirinus. By that deed he persuaded the people that Romulus had gone to the gods and freed the senate from the suspicion of regicide.
